quote: Die Auflösung der trinomischen Gleichung $x^m + x^n t + t = 0$ durch Modulfunctionen.
english: The solution of the trinomial equation $x^m + x^n t + t = 0$ by modular functions.
topic: A list of research problems: proving Dirichlet's habilitation theorems with ideal theory, representing integers as a square plus a cube via discriminants of cubic fields and complex multiplication, solving trinomial equations with modular functions, the class number of pure cubic fields, and a question about composing quadratic fields.

triage.modern_statement: Express the roots x(t) of the one-parameter trinomial family x^m + t·x^n + t = 0 (an algebraic function of t) in closed form using modular functions. This generalizes the classical case of the quintic, where the Bring–Jerrard form x^5 + x + t = 0 is solved with elliptic modular functions. Modern version: for general degrees, can the roots be written using modular functions (elliptic, or Siegel modular functions / theta constants of higher genus) composed with explicit transcendental inversions such as hypergeometric or hyperelliptic integrals?
triage.answered_by: Hermite (1858), with Kronecker and Brioschi, solved degree 5 (Bring–Jerrard form x^5+ux+v=0) using elliptic modular functions; Klein developed the method further. For general degree, Hiroshi Umemura solved any algebraic equation, trinomials included, with Siegel modular functions / theta constants. This appears as 'Resolution of algebraic equations by theta constants', an appendix to Mumford's Tata Lectures on Theta II (1984). A separate line of work gives closed-form roots of trinomials through hypergeometric series: Birkeland (papers up to 1927) and Mellin (1921).

evidence.claim: In 1858 Hermite published the first known solution of the general quintic using elliptic transcendents. Brioschi and Kronecker found equivalent solutions at about the same time. The method works on the Bring–Jerrard (trinomial) form.
Klein's method: the general quintic is reduced to Bring–Jerrard form, which can then be solved directly with elliptic modular functions.
Umemura solved algebraic equations of arbitrary degree with theta constants, using Siegel modular functions and hyperelliptic integrals. This is an appendix to Mumford's Tata Lectures on Theta II.
Umemura's appendix in Mumford's Tata Lectures explains how to solve algebraic equations; it is described as one of his famous works.
Classical research on solving trinomial equations was founded by Hermite, Kronecker, Birkeland, Mellin and Brioschi, and has been continued by others, including through hypergeometric functions.
Mellin (1921) gave an integral formula, using hypergeometric functions of the coefficients, for the principal root of polynomial equations of trinomial and multinomial type.
Birkeland published papers solving algebraic equations with hypergeometric series, ending with his 1927 paper.

triage.why: The note is a short program item. It extends the Hermite–Kronecker–Klein solution of the Bring–Jerrard quintic by elliptic modular functions to general trinomials x^m + t x^n + t. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems as stated. It is related to his 13th problem, which is about solving equations of degree 7 by superposition of functions, but I don't have a source linking this note directly to that problem. The broad question was answered: Umemura (1984) solved general algebraic equations with Siegel modular functions / theta constants, and Birkeland and Mellin had already given explicit hypergeometric solutions for trinomials. I found no source saying Hilbert himself carried out the program in this exact form. Sources also don't say whether elliptic modular functions alone could handle every m and n, so the verdict is 'solved' only in the generalized (Siegel modular) sense. Recent papers on hypergeometric and modular solutions of trinomials and quintics, such as the 2021 ResearchGate and arXiv papers cited here, show that people are still working on this.
